faq.a: Impaired baroreflex fails to buffer the gravitational shift, leading to excessive sympathetic activation and vasoconstriction.
faq.q: Why does blood pressure rise on standing in this condition?

faq.a: Some agents (e.g., decongestants, certain herbal stimulants) increase sympathetic tone and may precipitate the rise.
faq.q: Can antihypertensive drugs cause orthostatic hypertension?

faq.a: Yes, they reduce venous pooling and blunt the sympathetic surge, helping to control the orthostatic BP rise.

exam: A 58‑year‑old diabetic presents with headache on standing. What bedside test confirms orthostatic hypertension? — Measure BP supine, then at 1 and 3 minutes after standing; a rise ≥20/10 mmHg confirms.

How would you differentiate orthostatic hypertension from orthostatic hypotension in a patient with dizziness? — Look at direction of BP change; hypertension shows a rise, hypotension a fall, and symptoms differ (headache vs syncope).
Which medication class is first‑line to blunt the sympathetic surge and why? — Beta‑blockers; they reduce heart rate and peripheral vasoconstriction without causing further volume overload.

A patient on herbal weight‑loss supplements develops orthostatic hypertension. What is the likely mechanism? — Stimulant herbs increase catecholamine release, amplifying sympathetic response on standing.

In a low‑resource hospital without tilt‑table, how can you reliably assess orthostatic BP? — Use a manual sphygmomanometer, measure after the patient sits for 5 minutes, then after standing for 1 and 3 minutes.
What are the long‑term risks if orthostatic hypertension is left untreated? — Accelerated atherosclerosis, left‑ventricular hypertrophy, stroke, and increased cardiovascular mortality.
Why should ACE inhibitors be used cautiously in a patient with renal impairment? — They can worsen renal function if baseline GFR is low; monitor creatinine and potassium.

A patient with HIV presents with orthostatic hypertension. What additional work‑up is warranted? — Screen for autonomic neuropathy (heart‑rate variability), assess CD4 count, and rule out opportunistic infections affecting the nervous system.
ai.title: Orthostatic Hypertension
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Orthostatic hypertension is a rise in blood pressure upon standing, opposite to orthostatic hypotension. It signals autonomic dysfunction or volume overload and can increase cardiovascular risk.

b: Prevalence higher in older adults, diabetics, and patients with chronic kidney disease.
Associated with increased risk of stroke, myocardial infarction, and mortality.
sections.p: When a patient moves from supine to standing, systolic BP rises ≥20 mmHg or diastolic BP rises ≥10 mmHg. This abnormal response reflects impaired baroreflex or excess sympathetic drive.

b: Diagnostic criteria: ΔSBP ≥20 mmHg or ΔDBP ≥10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing, measured on at least two occasions.
Pathophysiology: baroreceptor resetting, heightened sympathetic tone, volume overload, or medication effect.
sections.p: The diagnosis rests on repeated orthostatic BP measurements and exclusion of confounders such as recent caffeine, pain, or anxiety.

b: Complications: hypertensive crisis, left‑ventricular hypertrophy, renal impairment.
Urgent red flag: sudden severe headache or visual loss suggesting hypertensive emergency.
sections.p: Patients may present with headache, palpitations, or visual blur on standing. In low‑resource settings, consider malaria, HIV‑related autonomic neuropathy, or chronic anemia as contributors.

t.b: Confirms the magnitude of rise; a rise ≥20/10 mmHg meets criteria.
Detects renal dysfunction or electrolyte shifts that may amplify BP rise.
Identifies uncontrolled diabetes, a common cause of autonomic neuropathy.
Looks for left‑ventricular strain or arrhythmias that may be precipitated by BP spikes.
Screen for chronic kidney disease when laboratory services are limited.

b: Remove or adjust offending drugs (e.g., decongestants, NSAIDs).
Low‑salt diet and gentle fluid restriction if volume overload suspected.
Beta‑blockers (e.g., propranolol) to blunt sympathetic surge; avoid in asthma.
ACE inhibitors or ARBs if hypertension persists; monitor renal function.
Non‑pharmacologic: gradual position changes, compression stockings.
sections.p: Treat underlying cause first, then modulate sympathetic activity and volume status.

b: Distinguish by measuring both BP and pulse on standing.
In orthostatic hypotension, symptoms are dizziness and syncope; in hypertension, symptoms are headache or visual changes.
sections.p: Orthostatic hypotension, which shows a fall in BP on standing, and postural tachycardia syndrome, where heart rate rises >30 bpm without a BP rise.

b: Always repeat measurements after the patient rests for 5 minutes.
Use automated devices validated for orthostatic testing when possible.
sections.p: White‑coat effect may exaggerate supine BP, masking the orthostatic rise. Dehydration can blunt the expected rise, leading to false‑negative results.

b: Ask about recent infections (malaria, TB) that may affect autonomic function.
Check for peripheral neuropathy in HIV or diabetic patients.
sections.p: Focus on bedside orthostatic BP, medication review, and signs of autonomic neuropathy (dry skin, gastroparesis).

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden severe headache, visual loss, or neurological deficit indicating hypertensive emergency.
